query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Atomic layer deposition can deposit a precisely controlled surface coating that, upon mild oxidation at high temperature, forms a continuous and dense protective oxide layer, thereby improving the oxidation resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with an uncoated surface
generation.intervention: Application of a surface coating via atomic layer deposition, with optimized composition and thickness tailored for high-temperature oxidation conditions
generation.conditions: Exposed to oxidative atmospheres at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 1000–1100 °C) for long durations
generation.structural_mediator: A protective oxide layer that forms on the ALD coating (such as a dense CrTaO4-based or similar stable oxide), which acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress
generation.mechanism: The ALD process allows for nanometer-scale control of the coating parameters. The optimized coating, when exposed to high-temperature oxidation, forms a stable and continuous oxide layer that restricts oxygen diffusion into the bulk material, thus mitigating further oxidation of the substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated RHEA samples will exhibit a lower oxidation rate (evidenced by reduced weight gain and improved oxide layer integrity) compared to uncoated samples under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.baseline: RHEA specimens without any surface coating
generation.boundary: The oxidation resistance improvement is expected to hold as long as the coating remains dense, continuous, and adherent under the targeted high-temperature conditions; deviations in coating integrity could lessen the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of oxidation resistance improvement depends on the specific coating composition, thickness, and long-term stability at extreme temperatures, and optimal parameters may vary with different RHEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of RHEA samples: one group will receive an ALD-deposited coating with controlled composition and thickness, while the control group will remain uncoated. Both groups will be subjected to isothermal oxidation at elevated temperatures (e.g., 1100 °C) for an extended duration (e.g., 200 hours).
measurements: Weight gain per unit area as a measure of oxidation extent
Oxide scale morphology and continuity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase and chemical composition of the oxide layer using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., weight gain, oxide spallation) or fail to form a continuous protective oxide compared to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis that ALD-deposited coatings enhance oxidation resistance via formation of a protective oxide layer will be falsified.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ].
